title: 2 Samuel 12:1–15
context: This section is kept whole. The LORD sends the prophet Nathan, who tells David a parable of a rich man who took a poor man’s only lamb. David pronounces judgment on the rich man, and Nathan answers that David is the man. Speaking for the LORD, Nathan recounts God’s gifts to David, names his sins against Uriah and Bathsheba, and announces that the sword will not depart from his house and that public calamity will come from within his own family. David confesses that he has sinned against the LORD. Nathan answers that the LORD has put away his sin and he will not die, but that the child will die because the deed has given the LORD’s enemies occasion to blaspheme. Both traditions see here real sin, real rebuke, real confession, real forgiveness and real consequences. Psalm 51, whose title links it to Nathan’s coming to David, is widely read as David’s response. The traditions differ on how they describe a grave fall in a believer, noted at verse 13.

verses.text: The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him, and said to him, “There were two men in one city: the one rich, and the other poor.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sends Nathan to David, and Nathan begins a story of two men in one city, one rich and one poor. God takes the initiative.

Arminian readers note that God’s sending of Nathan is grace that seeks the sinner, calling David to repentance while he can still respond, and that God does not abandon even a gravely fallen servant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD’s initiative in sending the prophet shows that restoration begins with God, not with the sinner; David had hidden his sin, but God would not let it stay hidden.

Both traditions see Nathan’s mission as an act of God’s mercy as well as of his judgment, and see faithful rebuke as a gift.

verses.text: The rich man had very many flocks and herds,
verses.arminianNotes:
The rich man has very many flocks and herds. Nathan establishes the rich man’s abundance.

Arminian readers note that the parable invites David to judge by his own moral sense before he realizes he is the subject, a wise way of letting conscience speak before self-defense can rise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the rich man’s abundance mirrors the many gifts God had given David, which Nathan will list in verse 8, so that David’s sin is shown to be not need but greed against a God who had given generously.

Both traditions read the detail as setting up the contrast of power and vulnerability at the heart of the parable.

verses.text: but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The poor man has only one little ewe lamb, which he bought and raised; it grew up with his children, ate his food, drank from his cup, lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him. The lamb is cherished.

Arminian readers note that the tender detail draws the hearer’s sympathy to the poor man and the lamb, and that the parable casts Bathsheba as the innocent lamb, not as a guilty party.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the lamb lying in the poor man’s bosom echoes the language of verse 8, and that the image presents Uriah’s marriage as a loving bond that David violated; some interpreters also hear a play on the word for daughter in Bathsheba’s name.

Both traditions read the parable as placing Bathsheba among the wronged, not the wrongdoers.

verses.text: A traveler came to the rich man, and he didn’t want to take of his own flock and of his own herd to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When a traveler visits, the rich man will not take from his own flocks but takes the poor man’s lamb and prepares it for his guest. The injustice is stark.

Arminian readers note that the rich man’s act is a free and selfish choice, exactly like David’s, and that the parable exposes the abuse of power by the strong against the weak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parable focuses on the taking of the lamb, highlighting that David’s sin was theft of another man’s wife by royal power, a violation of the commandments against coveting and stealing (Exodus 20:15, 17).

Both traditions see the parable as a mirror held up to David so that he will condemn his own act before he knows it is his.

verses.text: David’s anger burned hot against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
verses.arminianNotes:
David burns with anger at the rich man and swears by the LORD that the man deserves to die. David’s sense of justice is still alive.

Arminian readers note that David’s conscience is not dead; he can recognize injustice clearly in another, which shows that the call to repentance still has something to work on in him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s swift condemnation shows how easily sinners judge others while blind to the same sin in themselves, a pattern Paul warns against (Romans 2:1).

Both traditions see David’s anger as the moment the trap of the parable closes, and both observe that his verdict will fall on his own head.

verses.text: He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity!”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says the man must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this and had no pity. David cites the law.

Arminian readers note that David applies the law of restitution for stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), showing he knows God’s standards, which makes his own violation the more culpable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase had no pity condemns David’s own heartlessness toward Uriah, and that some interpreters, ancient and modern, have connected the fourfold restitution with later sorrows in David’s family, though the text does not make that link.

Both traditions read David’s verdict as an unwitting self-judgment.

verses.text: Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan says to David that he is the man, and then speaks the LORD’s word: God anointed him king over Israel and delivered him from Saul. The parable turns on David.

Arminian readers note that God’s word confronts David personally and directly, and that his responsibility is undeniable; God names his grace first, so the sin is seen against the backdrop of what God had given.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD recounts his sovereign acts, I anointed and I delivered, so that David’s sin appears as ingratitude against God’s free favor; the rebuke is grounded in grace.

Both traditions treat Nathan’s words as shared ground: God’s prophet rightly rebukes even the king, and sin is first an offense against God’s goodness.

verses.text: I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things.
verses.arminianNotes:
God says he gave David his master’s house and wives, and the house of Israel and Judah, and would have given still more if that had been too little. God’s generosity was abundant.

Arminian readers note that God’s willingness to give even more shows that David’s sin was not driven by lack, and that God desires to bless his people generously when they walk with him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the language of giving into David’s bosom echoes the parable’s lamb in the poor man’s bosom, so that David is shown to have taken what God had not given while despising what he had. The reference to Saul’s wives may describe royal transfer of the household; its details are uncertain.

Both traditions read this verse as exposing sin as ingratitude toward a generous God.

verses.text: Why have you despised the LORD’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes:
God asks why David despised the LORD’s word by doing evil, striking Uriah with the sword, taking his wife, and killing him with the Ammonites’ sword. The charges are named.

Arminian readers note that the root of David’s sin is despising God’s word, and that sin against neighbors is at bottom a rejection of God’s authority; David used the enemy’s sword, but the murder is counted as his.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God names both adultery and murder plainly, using the language of 11:27 about what is evil in his sight, and that no human cover-up can hide what God sees.

Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground: David’s guilt is clear, and neither tradition excuses him.

verses.text: Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore the sword will never depart from David’s house, because he despised God and took Uriah’s wife. The judgment fits the crime.

Arminian readers note that consequences follow sin even when forgiveness will be granted, and that David’s choices will bring real suffering on his family in the chapters that follow (13:28–29; 18:14–15; 1 Kings 2:25).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the sword David used against Uriah returns upon his own house, an example of God’s measured justice, and that this judgment stands even after David is forgiven.

Both traditions agree that forgiveness does not erase all earthly consequences, and both read the violence in David’s family as the outworking of this word.

verses.text: “This is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will raise up evil against David from his own house and give his wives to his neighbor, who will lie with them in broad daylight. The judgment mirrors the sin.

Arminian readers note that the punishment corresponds to David’s offense, showing that God’s justice is fitting, and that this was fulfilled when Absalom took his father’s concubines (16:21–22).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s statement that he will raise up evil does not make God the author of Absalom’s sin; God governs and uses wicked human acts as judgment while those who commit them remain guilty.

Both traditions read the verse with sobriety and affirm both God’s justice and human responsibility.

verses.text: For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
God says that David acted secretly, but God will do this before all Israel and before the sun. Hidden sin will meet public judgment.

Arminian readers note that the contrast between secret sin and public consequence shows that God will not allow wrong to remain hidden, and calls believers to bring their sins into the light through confession.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s knowledge of secret sins is complete, and that he governs history so that what is done in secret is brought to light, as Jesus also taught (Luke 12:2–3).

Both traditions see this verse as shared ground: nothing is hidden from God, and his judgment on David’s sin will be visible.

verses.text: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has put away your sin. You will not die.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says to Nathan that he has sinned against the LORD, and Nathan answers that the LORD has put away his sin and he will not die. Confession meets forgiveness.

Arminian readers note that David’s confession is a genuine turning back to God, and that his restoration shows God’s readiness to forgive the penitent after a grave fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s confession is the fruit of God’s grace working through Nathan’s rebuke, and they see the discipline that follows as God’s means of restoring and preserving him.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian and Reformed readers agree that David’s forgiveness was real and that its consequences were also real (12:10–14), and both commend Psalm 51, whose title links it to this event, as the fitting response. They differ on what such a grave fall means for a believer. Classical Arminians typically hold that grave, willful sin truly endangers a believer’s standing before God, and that David’s repentance restored him. Reformed readers typically hold that a regenerate person can fall grievously but not finally, and that God’s discipline and Nathan’s rebuke were the means by which God preserved him.

verses.text: However, because by this deed you have given great occasion to the LORD’s enemies to blaspheme, the child also who is born to you will surely die.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan says that because the deed has given the LORD’s enemies great occasion to blaspheme, the child born to David will die. Consequences remain after forgiveness.

Arminian readers note that public sin by God’s people damages God’s reputation among unbelievers, and that the consequences announced here show the seriousness of sin even when forgiveness has been granted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the WEB wording speaks of giving the LORD’s enemies occasion to blaspheme. Some commentators suggest a harsher original phrase about scorning the LORD himself; these notes do not settle that question, and the verse as printed stresses the dishonor brought on God’s name.

Both traditions read this as real forgiveness alongside real consequences, a hard word that the following verses handle with grief rather than detachment.

verses.text: Then Nathan departed to his house. The LORD struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, and he was very sick.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan goes home, and the LORD strikes the child Uriah’s wife bore to David, and he becomes very ill. The narrator still calls her Uriah’s wife.

Arminian readers note that the child’s illness is grievous, and that readers should approach it with humility and compassion rather than easy explanations, recognizing that David’s sin brought suffering on the innocent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD is named as acting in the child’s illness, consistent with his sovereignty over life and death, while the guilt for the circumstances lies with David, not the child. The phrase Uriah’s wife keeps the wrong before the reader.

Both traditions treat the verse with sorrow and refuse to make the child a symbol rather than a person.
